title: A quantum unstructured search algorithm for discrete optimisation: the use case of portfolio optimisation
abstract_summary: The authors introduce QSERA, a quantum unstructured search algorithm that locates extrema or roots of discrete objective functions by mapping f(x) to a binary oracle u(z) (via rescaling and powering) and then applying Grover's algorithm for O(√N) search. QSERA supports higher-than-quadratic objective terms (beyond QUBO), requires knowledge or estimates of f_min and f_max (but can work approximately when these are inexact), and the paper demonstrates gate constructions and a portfolio optimisation use case with an explicit quantum circuit.
methodology_description: The authors propose QSERA, a quantum unstructured-search based method to find extrema and roots of discrete objective functions. Methodologically they: (1) express the discrete objective f(x) in a binary-variable polynomial form (allowing up to K-th order terms), (2) rescale f(x) to g(x) in [0,1] using (known or estimated) fmin and fmax (different formulas for minimisation, maximisation, root finding), (3) raise g(x) to an integer power n to create un(z) ≈ u(z) that acts as a Boolean oracle (u(z*)=1, u(z≠z*)=0 in the n→∞ limit), (4) map binary variables to qubit-basis states and represent single-bit projector operators Bk = 1/2(I − Zk), (5) construct Gn = sum_j Cj (polynomial terms) so that Gn |z⟩ = g(x)^n |z⟩ and implement Q* = exp(iπGn) as a product of controlled phase gates (multi-controlled P(ϕ) operations implemented with ancillas/AND constructions), (6) implement the complementary diffusion operator Q+ (Hadamard-based reflection) and run Grover iterations (Q+ Q*)^m with m ≈ (π√N − 2)/4 to amplify the target state amplitude. They derive the explicit decomposition of the required gates (phase rotations, multi-controlled phases, Toffoli decomposition down to H, X, Z, P, T) and show how to compute the coefficients cn, cn,i, ... recursively from g(x). The methodology is demonstrated on a synthetic portfolio-optimisation instance (Na=4 assets) where f(x) is defined to track benchmark return and volatility with a soft budget constraint; the circuit uses 4 data qubits, ancillas for multi-controls and phase-tracking, and is executed on a zero-noise Qiskit simulator to evaluate success probabilities as a function of oracle power n and Grover iterations.
algorithms_used: QSERA (Quantum Search for Extrema and Roots Algorithm)
experimental_setup: Classical zero-noise statevector simulator from Qiskit (version 1.0). The quantum circuits were constructed and decomposed to basic gates (H, X, Z, P, T, Toffoli) and executed on a noiseless simulator.
dataset_used: Synthetic toy financial dataset: Na = 4 assets with specified expected returns µ = [0.05, 0.01, 0.02, 0.04], volatilities σ = [0.40, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30], and 4x4 correlation matrix ρ as given in the paper. Benchmark target µ_b = 0.043, σ_b = 0.195, and budget Nb = 2 (choose 2 assets).

experiment_input.preprocessing: Formulate objective f(x) (Eq. 33) as multi-order polynomial, rescale to g(x) using chosen fmin/fmax (authors used fmin ≈ 0, fmax ≈ 0.15), expand g(x) to compute coefficients c1, c1,i, ... and recursively compute coefficients for g(x)^n (cn, cn,i,...). Map binary selection vector x to integer z (qubit basis).

pipeline_steps: Define the discrete objective f(x) for portfolio tracking (Eq. 33) and express it as a polynomial in binary variables.
Choose/estimate fmin and fmax and rescale f->g in [0,1] (minimisation formula used in example).
Select oracle power n and compute g(x)^n coefficients recursively to build Gn = Σ Cj where Cj are j-th order operator terms.
Represent single-bit projectors Bk = 1/2(I − Zk) and build multi-qubit controlled-phase operators Pj(ϕ) for each Cj term, using ancilla-based AND constructions where needed.
Assemble Q* = exp(iπ Gn) and diffusion operator Q+, decompose to elementary gates (H, X, Z, P, T, Toffoli).
Initialise qubits in uniform superposition with Hadamards and apply (Q+ Q*)^m with m ≈ (π√N − 2)/4 (mopt; for N=16 mopt=2), then measure computational basis.
Vary oracle power n (authors explored up to ≈40 and used n=24 in examples) and record probability of measuring the optimal portfolio; analyse trade-off between n and success probability.

experiment_output.format: Probability distribution over computational-basis measurement outcomes (each basis state = a portfolio).
metrics: Probability of measuring the target (optimal) portfolio state
Success probability as a function of oracle power n

experiment_output.observations: Optimal portfolio 1001 had the highest measurement probability (but <1 because fmin/fmax were estimated). The second-best portfolio (0101) had the next-highest probability. Success probability depends non-monotonically on the oracle power n: small n insufficiently distinguishes the optimum, intermediate n (≈20–30 in the example) maximises success, large n drives all un(z)→0 and success probability drops.

reproducibility_notes: The paper provides full algorithmic description, explicit asset parameters, formulae for coefficient computation, and decompositions of quantum gates down to elementary gates. The authors state that quantum computations were performed on a classical zero-noise Qiskit simulator (version 1.0). No code repository or data files are provided in the manuscript, so reproduction would require reimplementation of the described circuit construction and recursive coefficient computation using the provided formulas and appendix tables.

results_summary: The authors propose QSERA, a method to reduce discrete extremum/root-finding problems to an unstructured search by constructing an oracle u(z) from a scaled objective g(x) (via g(x)^n) and then applying Grover amplification. They derive how to express arbitrary K-th order objective functions as quantum phase operators and give explicit multi-controlled phase gate constructions. A worked portfolio-optimisation example with Na=4 assets is implemented in a zero-noise Qiskit simulator: the constructed oracle and subsequent Grover iterations amplify the target portfolio state's measurement probability; the authors show how the oracle exponent n controls discrimination of the optimum when fmin/fmax are only estimated. The paper highlights practical caveats: the cost of computing the oracle parameters and the circuit depth may be large and can limit real-world advantage, and knowledge of global bounds affects single-shot certainty.
performance_claims: Quadratic speed-up for the search stage: O(√N) iterations via Grover (standard theoretical Grover bound).
Optimal number of Grover iterations m_opt ≃ (π√N − 2) / 4 (standard formula used in the paper).
Example scale: with Na ~ 10^5 assets the search space size is 2^Na (paper cites 2^105 for Na≈10^5 and approximates this as ~10^30,000), illustrating intractability classically.
Worked numerical example: Na = 4 (N = 16) so m_opt = 2 Grover iterations were used in the simulation.

Oracle exponent effects: in the portfolio example the authors find empirically in simulation that moderate n in the range ~20–30 gives effective discrimination of the optimum, whereas too large n drives oracle amplitudes to zero (figured behavior).
The objective function in the example is expanded up to 4th order; parameter tables for c_{n,...} coefficients are provided (numerical values listed in the paper).
quantum_advantage_detail: The authors claim QSERA achieves the usual quadratic speed-up of Grover's search (O(√N)) for the search component; this is a theoretical advantage contingent on an efficient implementation of the oracle. The paper does not demonstrate a practical end-to-end quantum advantage on real hardware, and it explicitly notes that the classical cost and circuit depth of mapping f(x) → u(z) (oracle construction) may negate or limit the benefit in practice.
limitations: QSERA requires a priori knowledge of the global minimum and maximum (fmin and fmax) of the objective function to guarantee finding x* with certainty; when these are not known only estimates can be used and the success probability falls below 1 (author-stated).

The mapping f(x) -> u(z) depends on raising a rescaled objective g(x) to a power n; choosing n too large can drive un(z) -> 0 for all z and destroy the oracle's ability to identify x*, so an appropriate (problem-dependent) n must be selected (author-stated).

The accuracy of the oracle and the circuit depth scale with the number of operations needed to compute the coefficients (cn, cn,i, cn,i1i2, ... ) for g(x)^n; computing these coefficients may be non-trivial and expensive for large problems (author-stated).

When fmin and fmax are only approximated, QSERA may only return approximate solutions (the most-likely measured states may be near the optimum) and multiple measurement shots are generally required to distinguish the true optimum (author-stated).

The quantum circuit depth grows with the degree/order of the objective (QSERA supports higher-than-quadratic terms), the power n used in the oracle construction, and the size of the problem, implying potentially large resource requirements (author-stated/inferred).

[inferred] The number of higher-order interaction terms grows combinatorially with the number of binary variables (K), so parameter expansion and gate construction likely scale poorly (exponential blow-up), limiting scalability to large instances.

[inferred] Deep circuits and many controlled-phase / multi-controlled gates (ancilla usage) required by QSERA make it vulnerable to noise and decoherence on NISQ hardware; practical implementations may be infeasible without significant error mitigation or future fault-tolerant devices.
[inferred] Precomputing the coefficients for g(x)^n on a classical computer may itself be computationally expensive (possibly exponential), offsetting the quantum search speedup for large K.

[inferred] The method maps discrete and discretised continuous problems to an unstructured search — for problems with exploitable structure (e.g., gradients), classical or other quantum structured algorithms (QAOA, VQE, adiabatic) may be more efficient; QSERA may be suboptimal when structure exists.

key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — QSERA maps discrete objective functions to a binary oracle via rescaling and integer powering, enabling the use of Grover-style unstructured search with theoretical O(√N) query complexity.

#idea:quantum-advantage — The method supports objective polynomials beyond QUBO (K-th order terms) by constructing Gn operators whose eigenphases encode g(x)^n, implemented with multi-controlled phase gates.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Classical preprocessing (computing f_min/f_max estimates and recursively deriving coefficients for g(x)^n) is required to construct the quantum oracle; the approach therefore uses classical pre/post-processing plus a quantum search core.

#idea:hybrid-approach — The authors provide an explicit gate-level decomposition (down to H, X, Z, P, T and Toffoli) and ancilla/AND constructions, illustrating how to implement Q* = exp(iπGn) and the diffusion operator.

#idea:quantum-advantage — Demonstrated on a toy 4-asset (N=16) portfolio-tracking instance using a noiseless Qiskit statevector simulator, reporting success probabilities as a function of oracle power n and Grover iterations m.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Observed a nontrivial trade-off between oracle power n and success probability (intermediate n maximises success; too large n causes collapse of amplitude separation when g(x)^n→0 for all non-optimal states).
contradictions: #contradiction:scalability — The paper asserts Grover-style quadratic speedup but provides only a noiseless simulation for N=16 (4 data qubits). The explicit gate decompositions and ancilla requirements imply deep circuits and substantial qubit overhead for larger problem sizes, undermining claims of practical scalability without fault-tolerant hardware.

#contradiction:scalability — The success probability depends sensitively and non-monotonically on the chosen oracle power n and on estimates of f_min/f_max; this parameter sensitivity complicates straightforward application of Grover amplitude amplification at scale and calls into question simple statements of advantage absent robust parameter-selection strategies.

#contradiction:scalability — No classical baselines or empirical noisy-hardware results are provided, so the claimed practical advantage over classical methods is not demonstrated and may not hold once realistic noise and resource costs are accounted for.
